blocks.x: Let's get your name. The first thing, just to test it out. What's your name? Luke Skiro. Luke Skiro?
Mm-hmm.
And this is the first reel. What's today's date? Is it December the...
December the 5th.
December the 5th, 1967?
Yeah.
And we're at 910 Royal Apartment 4th.
Right.
So, you want to tell me where you were born and when? Just to start off?
Well, I was born in New Orleans in 1911, September 24th.
1911, September 24th.
Yeah.
Well, you're still a young man. You're not like some of the musicians. I see it, right?
Well, I'm 56 years old. I just made 56. Mm-hmm.

I remember something I wanted to ask you before I forget it. How did you happen to remember all these nicknames of guys? Like Johnny Frisco, you told me he had a nickname. Yeah, Newfoot. Well, uh... You knew him well?

Yeah. He played with Buck Vandal on and off. And he was with... Happy Shilling for a long time. And some of Buck Vandal's band was with him also. Mm-hmm. And they all had nicknames, huh? Fonz? Fonz? Yeah, Fonz. Well, we used to call him Sack or Goat.
How come?

Well, because... A good while back in school, he brought a goat up to the classroom up on the third floor. And the teacher put him on his... He was always in some kind of a jam with the teachers or something. He was a character. They had him in opportunity class for a while. And... He was just a little too much for the teachers.
What's the opportunity, Glenn?

Let's see. How would I say it now? Uh... He was sort of low on some of his, you know, prayers. And they were, you know, trying to find out why. I don't know. In fact, it was bugging him or something. Mm-hmm.
Oh, I see. And, uh... You said Jake Schamber had another nickname, too.
Yeah. He was... I think...
Fonz over the nickname that Putty knows a putty. Just call him Putty, huh?
Putty.
On account of his nose. Yeah. We can get back to you. I just... It's just something I wanted to get down before we forgot.
Yeah.
Uh... Whatever you... Wherever you want to start telling about your life. You know, did you come from a musical family? No. Nobody played music in front of you?
No. They all were hardworking folks. I mean, ice cream business. My dad was an ice cream business.
Well, that gave you an opportunity to hear a little music, I guess, huh?

Oh, yeah. I mean, uh... You told me. It was at the corner of my house there. The old man had an ice cream parlor there. And every Sunday there would be some Negro bands there. They would sort of meet each other and, you know, buck each other.
Mm-hmm.

And they would advertise for, like, dances and so forth. But it was, like, picnics or sales or something like that. And then they had these dances at night there at the economy hall of the center centers. And then they had the Astoria, the Capellet, you know, all those old halls, you know? Where were you going? Well, on St. Anne between, uh, Morewa and Liberty, just back at the auditorium, they had that old tone on since.
Near the Tremé Market.
Yeah, the Tremé Market. Yeah. There was a big open market there.
Yeah. And where was your daddy's ice cream place? It was on St. Philip and North Billeray.

Well, you never did move much away from that. No, and then after we had moved in the middle of the block, which was around, uh, let's see, between, uh, North Robison and North, you know, Burberry. All St. Philip Street, but in the middle of the block. And, uh, he got a big place there and he expanded some.
So you were close to Economy Hall and...
Yeah, I was up around the corner from the, uh, and around the corner from the Center Center. Yeah. And about a few blocks from the Interpreseverance. Mm-hmm.
And you heard the bands, didn't you? Oh, yeah, I heard a lot of them. Did you have any neighbors who played music that you used to listen to?

Well, my next door neighbor, his name was Big Eyed Lut. Mm-hmm. And, uh, I used to admire his style, but I was only about eight or nine years old. Yeah. And I still remember him. And around 15 years old, uh, I asked the old man to buy McLaren and he said, nope. So I had to beg for about two or three weeks. Finally, he got me a little cheap one for about thirty dollars. Mm-hmm. And I started to take lessons. I had, uh, started going to the Italian Hall there. Mm-hmm. And, uh, they had some old professor there. Uh, his name was, uh, was Kutcher, which was his last name. He used to charge me, it was like five hours a month. Professor Kutcher? Yeah.
I never did know him.

Yeah, I mean, uh, uh, uh, he started now, he was in the, uh, in the Contessa Antelina thing. Yeah. And then they had another professor there, uh, Professor Leaster, well, uh, uh, that came later, that. Was that the professor, you know, Kutcher College?
Was your father from Contessa Antelina?
Yeah, he was.
And what about... He and my mother too. Yeah. What about that name, Skiro, is that a, a, a, a, uh, Sicilian name, or, I mean, a, uh, Albanian, or? No, it's Albanian.
It's Albanian, no? Yeah, I had to, I had a big write-up on that. It's, it goes back to around Alexander the Great, I believe.
Yeah. I just wondered what kind of music was Albanian music, I've never heard it. Well, it's something like Italian music, yeah. Cinema. Yeah, cinema. Yeah.
Yeah.

Cause I know so many of the great clarinet players did come from Sicily. Yeah. And they're supposed to have good, uh, teaching there in Sicily, and a certain style of clarinet. Yeah. Well, Rapport was the city in his family.
Yeah, I'm almost sure he was.
Yeah. Cause all of his family, you know, tried to play the clarinet act, and there was a few

lay-ons there, I believe a couple of, you know, about three lay-ons there. And they all tried to, I mean, you know, they thought they could, it was, it felt like, a great rap, but it was impossible. And what about, there was a fan, too, he died, I think. Yeah, well, he was real good. He was a real good musician, but I guess liquor took all of him, like Fazolo. Yeah. But he was a fine musician. Fazolo liked to drink, huh? Yeah, he did drink a lot, too. He used to drink, gee, with, you see, gin with beer chasers and so forth. Yeah. He was actually a beatnik at all, I don't know. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm.

Well, you could tell he loved to eat, that's for sure. Yeah. I mean, he'd go home at night, he'd get a big head of lettuce and just chop it up. And he'd just eat that for supper, I mean, I meant to say, for snack. And then he'd, you know, sort of buy these dime novels and just read and read all through the night. And that's how he got most of his education. Yeah. Because he'd go extra high in school, I mean, he was just up around the sixth grade, I think, at the time. Mm-hmm.
I guess he just didn't care about too many things.

No, just liked his blues, liked his women in music. Well, that was very good. Yeah. There was nothing wrong with that. Yeah. Well, if he liked you, Paul, you were in. But if he didn't like you, that was it. Mm-hmm. He couldn't get along with a crim at all. We were all nervous. I just couldn't figure it out.
Did you know Fars before you started playing music?
Yeah, in school.
Did you go to listen to music with him before you started playing? Yeah, did you bomb around together? Yeah, we were.

We used to make the homebrew joints and all, and the fine, and the Arcadia, the Levita and all. We used to listen to him, and I showed him the finger on my old Albus system that I had. And this side of the week, he started learning the whole thing. You know what I mean? He was really good at it. You got started on clarinet? See, I started Farsola off on the clarinet.
Yeah, and you started on clarinet first before you stood up.

Yeah, yeah. I was in the main time I had bought a sacks from Jules Perdue. He was salesman at the time at C.J. Conn, and he sold me a fine sacks there. So I decided to have Fars that showed me the finger on the sacks. So he showed me the finger, and in the meantime, I went to a professor Sanders, and that's the professor that Farsola went to. What's his name? His name was Sanderson. Dan Sanderson.
Did he play with Schilling? Is that the guy? Maybe. Same time Dan Taggart did. I think I saw his picture in this book. Yeah.

So what I'm saying? He was a real fine old teacher. A lot of patience. And sometimes Farsola would get stuck, and he'd just hold his hand on his lap. The whole hour he says, okay Fars, if you didn't want to study, if you have hours up you can go. I'm going to have to leave him out of nowhere. He just wouldn't budge. And all of a sudden, about a year after, he went through, you see about three of these here, books. Is it like a method? Yeah. See, three methods inside of a year. He completed that and he was, I mean he surprised the prof and everybody around him. Was that on clarinet or sax or both? Sax on sax at the time. And then I used to loan him out clarinet for jobs. And then after that finally, he bought his own. What kind of sax did he start out on? He started out on a C melody. And then from a C melody, he bought a soprano. And from soprano, well he bought a clarinet and alto and a baritone sax and a tenor sax. He had the whole family. And then he started to play a little flute. And his sister was taking some piano lessons and she wasn't interested. So father was right there and he picked up on the piano and he started to play a little piano and some trombone and trumpet. And then he and Jay Shambin, I think it was you, Lamar, they went to... The Loyola School of Music band, they opened the door. They started home with transposition and fair and all. Boy they were great. And then every now and then, it was on a Sunday morning, they would say, Ed Fazzola and Jake Shambin would call and they all performed and they'd have some arrangements that they made up. And they'd ask me to listen to them. And they were real fun. They're real fun.
Mm-hmm.
A lot of notes here.
Yeah, well, how did Fazzola get that nickname?

Well, from Lloyd Primer. Just one night we were over at the Wittaginal on the Thursday night it was. And Lloyd Primer was looking for Fazzola and someone said, he's over at the Wittaginal, he said, oh, you mean Fazzola? And let's see. The name of Fazzola is actually for Bean, it's Bean in Italian in the words. It's a Fabio Bean they call it. And Lloyd Primer took all of that in Fazzola because he took Fazzola music. He said the name stuck. So in the meantime, Fazz came back and he started to call Lloyd Feet. Feet, huh? Feet, yeah. Because he had a set of hands on him on so bad. Every time he played the trumpet, he'd stomp his feet and all. He'd make just some feet there. So Fazzola and his feet.
Is your right name Luke? Yeah, Luke. Your full name, what is that? Just Luke Skiro? No middle name right?

Yeah, it was L. Just Lawrence Skiro. Yeah. It was around 1928 we used to make the home group joints and all the house parties and dances. And I had another good friend from school also. His name was Winnie Straley. Handsome boy. He looked something like Clark Apple. He was a fine sex man. He also took from Dan Sanderson at the same time. And Harry Shields taught him how to use the chords. And he turned out to be a real fine sex man. In the meantime his wife made it quick. I thought he was too handsome. That was his trouble. Yeah, and all of you.
That was censored. Okay, we're talking about Winnie Straley. Yeah. And how he played.

Well, he played sax mostly and he was real good. He was a good reading man in the section. And there was also another boy up from school, Slim Mayes or Francis Mayes. We used to call it an antidote. And he played a fine sex but he would never read.
Slim Mayes?
Yeah, you know, Francis Mayes.
I used to know him. He used to play bebop around the corner. That's the same guy, sort of?
Yeah, him.
What happened to him? Did he die?
No, no, no. He didn't die. I think he was running an oil station somewhere.
Well, he may be better off.
Yeah, because he took a couple of drinks and that was it. He was just gone.
Yeah.
So we named him an antidote because he looked like an antidote. Yeah. I mean, we had a nickname, we had a nickname of the Winnie Straley. What do you call him Flaxseed? Flaxseed?
Flaxseed, yeah. I've never heard of that. Well. What was a homebrew, John? Anyhow, I don't know that. What did you call him Flaxseed? Oh, there. Down in the back.

The homebrew, John? Well, I sold homebrew them. It was doing prohibition. They didn't have anybody's house, anything. There's any little hole in the wall there. They just set up, put the top, ice it up with icing. You had your homebrew there for twenty-five or fifteen cents a bar, whatever it was. You used to have these house parties and all that. Always had your homebrew and all that. You used to have some good times.
And the musicians would come in and play at these things? Oh yeah. Did they dance to music lights in there?
Oh yeah.
And the party that people would... What kind of dancing did they do? Did they do the Charleston then or that was after the dance?

Yes. I think it was after Charleston. Black body and all that. Fuzz trot, waltzes and all the girls. I just wanted to get back over to the military band. It was the Italian band. It was every Sunday morning we used to go to rehearsals there. It was from about nine to twelve. Like we learned a lot. I used to have to drag Fuzzola out of bed then. And he used to make it with me. And sometime back there was a plane of March. I think it was Starling Strikes Forever. And Fuzzola was hitting some hot legs up in there. And Professor heard the thing. But he wasn't sure. So he played it back. And he hurt Fuzzola again. So he drew the baton at Fuzzola. And Fuzz started to laugh like a fool. Everybody laughed and then he got a big kick out of it. I don't know, he was something. And then on, well Thursday night we used to... I went to Tessa and Delina band. We used to make all these parades and concerts and all the parcs. Which park was that? City park. City park. Yeah. It was real nice. And about 1933 I started to play at the St. Bernard Country Club with Tony Giardino. He had his wife on up here. Her name was Lou. And then there was a drum all-man Dick Cole. Dick Cole from Oklahoma. And the trumpet man was Wilkie Gerbright. And was on sax. They had Nat Geraci. And Tony Giardino and myself. And they had Johnny Sherman on drums. That was Johnny Sherman Sr. And they had the bass man. His last name was Legnan. I don't remember his first name. Was there any kind of Roscoe like that? I think it was him. Well it's the same guy. Yeah, the same guy. And no, at the same order, the country club I tell you was selling the beer. The beer was a nickel. The wine was a nickel. And high balls were done. And Buddy used to pack them in on that. By the way, which one of those Gerbicks was that?
That's Willie? Yeah, that's Willie, yeah. And that's the mothers, huh? Well, let's see. Pinky died. That was the oldest brother.
And they had Johnny. He had a heart attack. And so did Willie. I mean, they all had heart trouble. So I think they all quit playing.
What did Johnny play? He played drums and trumpet. And I heard Pinky played trumpet. Yeah. And I never heard him.

He played with the guitar. He was good. He was really good. A fine musician. In fact, sometimes he put the Shriners band. He does arranging and all for him. I think sometimes he leads the band at the Shriners at the Jerusalem Temple. Oh yeah. I guess when Mike Kaplan does it, he does it. I don't know if Mike does. Yeah. Yeah. And also I played the Sun Dodgers. That was with them. His name was Dan Mays on the sax. Show Duty on the drums. There was the chorus on the guitar and the piano man. His last name was Coim. His last name was Coyne. And we used to let the Dijks house a lot. And we used to broadcast about every week. I have the picture of that group home. I should have shown that too. You said that was a guitar player? No, it was a band-aid player. Who was it? His last name was Frondage.
He quit playing a long time ago. You're going to pull a lot of names I never heard of.

And then I also played with Arthur Selig Sr. at the St. Bernard Country Club after the Haunted Giordino level. We had a nice set up there. We had Arthur Selig Sr. on bass and guitar. And with Roz Zimmerman on piano. And Pierre Cirio. And with Paul Dana and myself on saxes. Charlie DuPont and I too. He was the Bupin on trumpet. And sometimes we had, on the drums we had, the boy's name, he was Lester Gauze. And then the other man that was something for him sometime was Leo Addy. He died too. Yeah. And Arthur Selig Sr. at the famous door number. And then also played at the Palm Court which was across the street in the Silver Slip at the time. And he played with Joe Gailer. You ever heard of him? No I don't know. He played a nice piano. Coats. You know, good chords. He and Henry Carubo on drums. And a little. Was he sometime. Whiffle was his name. I think. It was in relation to Stormy Rogers or something. He played drums? Yeah. He was a private thing boy, private thing.
There was Emmett and there was Buck Rogers.
I think it was Emmett, yeah. There was some relation up here. He played fine drums too.
I remember who you were talking about again. I heard of him. I'll ask Raymond Burke about it. I think Raymond thought about him. Wiffle Rogers. Yeah, we used to call him Wiffle.
Which one was Stew Meat Rogers? Yeah, Stew Meat. He's a good one. Same guy? It's a Nipper's Buck. Yeah. It's either Buck or Nipper.
Yeah. Well, maybe I got a picture up in here. Yeah. Keep talking, I'll find a picture.

And then I also played at the spotlight across the street from the famous Dill. We used to make it down at half the night and tips there. Hmm. Yeah. See, there was another band I also played with. That was with Jill Clessie, Tweety, Francis Murray. And Louis Caravello on drums. He's now playing bass. He's working for the railroad. Sometimes he comes out of height and sits in with us. Sometimes on the drums, sometimes on the bass. At Lodgins, huh? Yeah, let's see.
Here's a picture of Raymond Rogers. Yes. That's the one they call Wiffle? No.
No. No, he was extra thin blood.
Yeah. Yeah. Well, Buck was the uncle of Nett. Yeah. Of Nett. Yeah. So he was old, about a few years, I think. Buck was old, about a few years. Uh huh. Buck was old, Nett.

I remember when he died. And then we played at the old, let's see, the Roma Cafe, which was on Decatur Street. It was across the street from the Morning Call. It was the coffee shop there. Uh huh. See, it's a restaurant. It was upstairs, over the restaurant. There's a Roma restaurant there, yeah. Yeah, well, yeah. Well, that's the same spot upstairs. There was a beer joint there. Uh huh. And we had Arthur Sealy going banjo at the time. Uh huh. And, let's see, Joe Stevens on drums. That's the, look, Rag Baby Stevens' son.
Yeah, I heard him with Fuji Rack. Yeah. They played the footage right when Tony's Ron came in.

Yeah. And then, uh, we see, up there, Clara, and that's there, and sox. Uh huh. And then from there we went to the Wonder Bar on Decatur Street. They was at the Queer Joint. And, uh, we had, uh, let's see, Joe Stevenson's gang there. And Brett Dimmons on piano. And we had, uh, Tweety on trumpet, myself. And, uh, you know, they thought the band was, uh, they thought the band was, uh, queer so we quit. Uh huh. Well, and those places had been kept by the square. Yeah. And then there was another spot on Decatur Street. They used to call it Madame Reapers. Uh huh. She was a fortune teller. Uh huh. And, uh, we had a little three piece band there with a dollar and a half a night, as usual, and chips. Yeah. That's all you could get at the time. When was that?
During the Depression?

Around 1937. Uh huh. And then there was another place on Magazine Street. It's called Heavy's, Heavy's Seventh Heaven. And Bart smelled the high heaven. Heavy's Seventh Heaven? Yeah, with George E. And then they had the Green Goose on the list. On the, the, the, the name is Creepy. What do you say is Creepy? White Fair, I think. Yeah.
I don't know, I can't pronounce it.

Yeah, let's see. My playa dad just one night, and Harold Normandale, that was the Bad Bar in the Orleans at the time. Uh huh. He was in all kinds of trouble and all that. He came up with a sawed off shotgun. Yeah. And he started shooting up the joint. I jumped behind the pan, I quit that job.
I heard about, they had a place up there that was so tough, they put the band behind Chicken Wire. Yeah, oh that was, it was in the Audubon Park I believe.

Some place, I don't know, I'm kind of a little. Yeah. And then there was the Golden Dragon on St. Anne Street. Uh, the Slitko on piano, George Slitko, I haven't seen him for a long time. I think he was in California, he played a fine piano. Uh huh. And uh, we'll see Joe Stevens and myself, the three asses we used to call ourselves. Uh huh. And you know how we lost that, John? Uh huh. Well they had some girl around 18 years old, I was around 18 myself. Uh huh. And uh, they had some fine looking gal there, she sat on George's doctor, can him half a while, and moosed him a little, you know what I mean. Uh huh. She came over to me, almost, almost the uh, the bartender came from behind the public of 38. Uh huh. She said, you dare go so and so, I'm going to kill you. I said, why? I said, you messed up my girl. So man, I started to plead, man. Uh huh. A lot of a job that night again. Yeah. So we had a full round, she said, no, from there, let's see, I went to the Silver Star, which was on St. Claude and St. Bernard. The piano man, and he was, and so I was, uh, his name was, uh, Froger Schiffer. And they had, uh, you see the drum player, his name was Whipple, and that's the same thing. You know, the fellow was talking about. I see myself. And they had, they had some singing waiters there that was rockin' and rustle. And they also had the Negro Floor Shield. And that gun inside, Tyra was sitting with us. What did he play? He played sax, and I tried to teach him the clarinet, but his tone was so bad that he sort of gave it up. And then, and then, and then, and then from there we went, let's see, I was at, that, um, things were extra bad. So they had the ERA and the WPA and also, I got the WPA band. And I was in the military band there. And I had a few dance bands, and they were all, all of the best musicians in the city were on that thing at the time. It was just something that she always had in the pit, like, uh, Henry Raymond and, uh, some old professors, Gene Fonquet, the Papayas, the Chalvin DuPont, Charlie Cadela, Pete Bagova, one of them had bad boys, I used to call him Arthur Del Paget. He was a blackface comedian and drunk player. He had an Evolution Trio years ago. He didn't have, uh, too much nerve at the time. He used to do a lot of blackface. So he, Arthur Celia Gale, we sort of got together at the parks. We started at City Park and St. Rock, you know, Park, and the inner lot. And we used to have around, uh, two or three thousand, two or three thousand other people out there. So we did some blackface acts and he sort of broke me in. It was a lot of fun. I was almost frightened at that, but then, uh, uh, we had a little skit and, uh, we had a jumbo bottle full of, uh, this, you know, muscatel wine. Oh, yeah. And we had a little skit about wine and so forth. He sent me a little drink, Bloody. He used to call him Bloody, you know. Who do they call Bloody? Which one? Uh, uh, he bought bar and left. They both. People used to call each other Bloody. Oh, I see. And then we used to have a jam session in between there, you know. I'd say a half hour or just before the concert was over. We always had a jam session. Obviously, we were going to get to the guitar with Hyman on Susan Boone. Mm-hmm. And Bobo Arden on drums. And Henry Raymond on sax, myself on clarinet. And sometimes Charlie could go up with those sort of players. But he wasn't too, I mean, he didn't, uh, you know, care to play. He started out when I was young and I was trying and he didn't, you know. He was a guy like that. He was, he just got his kicks out of it, you know.

Well, he wanted to help you. He's a nice fellow Charlie. Yeah, yeah, he was one of the best guys I've ever known. I never did know Henry Raymond, but he made some nice records with Detroit. Yeah. Yeah. Let me fix us another drink. I'll have a take for about a while.
This is the second reel of Luke's Gero, December the 5th, 1967. He's just gonna talk while I make myself a drink.
Oh, my God. Talk about when I start getting in here.
We were talking about the Blackface Act. What kind of routine did you have?
Oh, just, how would I say it, no.
Did you have any jokes? Do you remember?

Yeah, a lot of jokes and all we had. I mean, I don't remember them all. I mean, it was... Taiwan, no more. Yeah, then, uh... We had a marching band up around the end of the concert. We'd see boys through the park and all the crowd would follow us, you know? Yeah. Something like the Saints or High Society. It was a lot of fun. I learned a lot out there, too. Some people would dance and all? Yeah, they're dancing there, you know, listening and everything else. And then we had some dance music and some marches and some light overtures and so forth. Oh, yeah. And I played with Buck Banville there, the American League. That's the old Plumpland. Yeah, that's...yeah. That's the, uh, Gentilly Post night, 203, or the Johnny Link's Post. What was in the band when you started that? Oh, there was... Arthur Duffy, yeah, that's Buh-Boy, that's on drums. And Bob Aguilar on the piano. Henry Connect on trumpet. And Fred Dante on the sides. And... What did Buck play? Oh, he also played the trumpet. They had a couple of trumpets, the Henry Connect, then Buck, then, uh... You see, Bob Aguilar died. So, so, so, but...so I took over on the piano. In the meantime, Henry got sick. So we hired Arthur Bubert. And then, uh, in the meantime, Dan Tagnan died, so we hired Leach. And, uh, he and I used to team up nice. I could, I could never get along with Dan too much, because he was up and down the sides. He was mechanical. And, uh, I just... He was a fine-sex man. And he used to overpower me. I mean, I had a soft to read. He had about a five read. I had about a two and a half. And he said, what the hell you blow loud? I said, well, it's the best I can do, Dan.
And he'd just get all frustrated. Can you still buy another five read? Do they still make them that hard?
No, I don't believe. I doubt it.
I never have known anybody that played a five read. Yeah.

It's a real hard read. Oh, I don't know how you did it. A four or three and a half, or three is, you know, average. I mean, if it might be set to have, no, you don't have to have those hard reads. Yeah. When I came... The layers are different. Yeah.
Do they have wider lay nouns?
Yeah, they're wider layers. You have to use a soft to read them. It all depends on the man behind it, too.
Yeah, well, I guess a wide lay would give you a bigger tone. Yeah, bigger tone, though. I don't know. But, let's see, about 1950 was when I first came out there.
Yeah.
And Otto Bubert on trumpet.
Yeah, Otto Bubert was on trumpet, fine trumpet man. And, uh...
Roland was on alto. Yeah, alto.

Roland Lee. And we had Charlie Fabry on drums. That's right. He also died. And then, uh... Well, we had a few substitutes like Buster, you got on drums. I don't know him. Well, I mean, he was a fine, you know, drummer. And then they had, you see, the three Mike Lawlers, I mean, each other had some good. A little black mic and a red mic. And also, old man Jack Assunto, a trombone. He played a few... And a lot of leaders, you know, tried to get that job by the time we grew up in the Union, but we had the job sewed up for 14 and a half years.
You had a good time.
Well, I knew that job wouldn't last, though.
I laughed he was good, too. Oh, he was one of the...
I think he was about the best in the punk and Susan Paul, myself.
Yeah, a lot of people say that, you know. Buck was playing piano then. I guess... Yeah. I don't remember what he sounded like on solos. Did he solo much out there?
No, just chord.
Yeah. Was he a good chord man?

Well, I mean, uh... He was hit and missed here, but I mean, uh... He had a good ear. Uh-huh. But I mean, he didn't know all the, you know, full changes. Uh-huh. And it helped, though. I mean, he, uh... He had that, uh, you know, steady, uh, full, full beat, you know? Yeah. And it helped a lot.
Yeah, well, that's what you want. It's a good rhythm, man.
Yeah, we had good rhythm there.
Yeah, we had good rhythm there. You ever play with a butterfly piano player? What you call a voodoo bell?

Oh! Oh! Oh! I played with one of those. I played with one of those again. The guys at some, uh, country club there. Boy, I thought the night would never end. So there was no rhythm at all. So we must think we lost that job. It was a battle and you lost, huh? Yeah, I know. So at the time I was playing with Johnny McDonnelly. But finally, I picked up on a fine piano man, Don O'Neill. Boy, he had a style like Teddy Wilson. He had a fine-look drum player. His name was, uh, who else is he? His name was Lee Tommy. Yeah, he drives a bus.

And then, I had been also playing with old Dominic Barocco. He's still playing the banjo and then there's this old violin player. He's a little bit of a guitar player. Henry Wilde, he plays fine guitar.

Oh, that was a good band. Oh, that was a good band. That was with, you know, Raymond Boyk and Charlie DuPont. The piano man was, let's see. I could see him right in front of me.
Was that before they had Chavez or after? No, it was, yeah, it was Julius Chavez, that's right. Oh, he was the one. Yeah.

The Melon Pickles. Yeah, the Melon Pickles. That's the band. And the drum? I used to listen to him every night over there. And the drum was pitch, you know? That was Al Domey? Yeah. Yeah. Al, well, is anything? The next time you see Al, ask him about Fazola. Yeah. And when he sees me, he says, the time I see you, I think of Fazola. Because we were always together, you know? Yeah. And he remembered that. Well, he also played at the Legion a couple of times with us. You know, Substituted? Mm-hmm. Boy, he plays a fine drums. And I played with the Marlis S. Cadillac a little bit. That's good in case they have any trouble. Yeah, they do.

Either that or jump over with one or two. Yeah. Been up there a long time with Johnny McDone. We used to call ourselves the Melody Man. We just spot around. We had a nice set up there. Good old band. He plays trumpet. He's a good spot and he's a real good man. Gets a beautiful tone too.
Does Hank Bellis ever sit in?

Yeah, names I just never heard of. I never heard of Speck Reagan that I know of. He's from New Orleans.

I don't think he was, but he used to sit in the arrogant and all. When you talk about piano players, there's a piano player that I'd like you to hear sometimes. He's a colored fellow. I knew his brother, but I never met him in time. Blackie, I knew him.

Yeah, but this boy was a handsome boy. He could pass the Spanish. He played with us a lot, but then he started to pull up that dope and that was it. He died young, but I don't remember him when he was four years old and playing piano. He couldn't even reach the pedals. He was a little bit of a piano player. They tried to make something out of him. Armstrong came in and heard him. A few of those big bands heard him and all. I don't want to learn how to read. But boy, he had a style. He'd make that piano rock. He was only about 112 pounds. Boy, I was talking about a man of a Harlem house. A hard society. Variations and all. And is he a wasn't even getting Pushy. He has a style or something like that. Yeah, but I'd like to hear him. In fact, he stayed at the house of Faisal who stayed in the noise line street. I think it was 19...07, I think. Or 1915.
Well I must know somebody from that neighborhood.
Well I mean, you can contact me and I can contact you for you.

Well you know, I heard a home-made record of Burnell about 9 days ago up in Little Rock, a guy named John Reed. See, he was a friend of Willie Santiago, who was an uncle. Yeah, Willie. She could get in touch with his widow because I found out when I was in office, that his widow had a lot of them. It must have been great.

Oh he was, he was tough. It was a shame that he had to go that fast. He used to stay up across the street in the house then. Boy they had all kinds of bands and every week. They had either a party or a fish fry or something else. And then there was another piano player, we used to call it Plutzum. He had a hunk, he was back on the hill. He played a fine piano. But this little Willie, I didn't see, I didn't know what this is. That's Push's uncle up, he played a very fine piano.
Very fine piano. You want some more eyes?
No.
God. How do you think you got your clarinets done?
Ah, no, I don't know. That's what I'm trying to figure out now. Who do I play like? I don't really know. I just play around and rather than that's it. Uh huh.

I played you that record when you came up to Tulane and Big Eye Louie. I don't think you quite sound like Big Eye Louie. No. You got a ratty tone. I don't know what kind of tone. Yeah, well I mean it's a jazz tone. It's not a legit tone. Yeah. Oh, when you were with Buck, you showed me that picture. Well, we got a copy of that picture. Yeah. The Buck Bandit. Where was that made?

That was in, I think it was in the Coventon. It was on the 4th of July. And we had a spot job. It was on the lakefront right out there. I don't quite remember the name of the place. But before a big fight started, so the sheriffs had troops of Teague, the ass around Aunt Florida. Everybody out there was dancing with tears in our eyes. You know that when Hank... You know, uh, you know Hank Kamen? What's that? Hank Kamen, he's a clarinet and saxophone player. He's from the way. No. He played on the president every Saturday night, so... When he sings... When he sings... Did he get over?
Hmm?

Oh, they have an invitation to you. Yeah, you know, you can't get over that. No, but... He, uh... He sings, I'm dancing with tears in my eyes because a girl in my arms is a boy. And nobody on the boat notices except a few old divers, you know. They don't ever catch it, you know. People don't ever listen to what's going on. They're too busy dancing on the boat.
They're trying to spook each other or something. Yeah. Did, uh...
Do you ever play many places where people don't dance?

Oh, that has happened a good while back. It was right there on the lakefront. Some American Legion home. Boy, we played all types of music. Latin American, Dixieland, cocktail or soft music, waltzes, everything. Even a polka we tried. Mm-hmm. But just about a couple or two, which I get up. So, it was intermission, uh... The leader went and he spoke to the band and asked him if there was anything wrong with the band. I said, no, everything is fine. Just keep on like they're doing, everything's fine. He said, hey, I tried... Oh, I had the music and I don't see anybody there. He said, here's what's happening. They haven't seen each other in a long time. They're all there chewing the fat right now. And sure enough, just before knocking off, they asked us if we wanted to make an hour overtime. Wow.

They must have lost it. Well, that was it. Well, how many places that you played didn't have dance floors at all that, you know, where people couldn't dance? Like on Bourbon Street, did they always have dance floors?
Well, they always had a little space to have to dance. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Because you know, Bear Gardens. I know now, you can't dance in the French Quarter.
No, you can't. And then you play the jazz club, they don't have dance in there. No dance in there either. Mm-hmm.

But all these spots sometimes have some dance in right now is... It's either the Bountaine Blue or the Bistro or in Legends or the Boat or Mont Leone or something like that. Yeah, that's just where Fugirat plays. Yeah, there's another one on there. Two-Nin-O-Vide to St. Rock in Medivitt, that's where we're at. Yeah, that's where we're at. There's no place on the West side.
No, not many spots.
No place on the West side. There's another side. It's here, but I'm not sure there's something there yet. It's a good while back there was the Wabbit before.

Yeah, but I think they don't play there. No, I think they don't play there. That's where we're at first. I tried to play with Johnny. McDonald? Yeah, Johnny McDonald. I know Bill Cray used to tell me he went over there and played with Mike Trepanie. Yeah. He was in the city the other night. Mike?

Yeah, he and Joe Steve. They're not doing it. I don't know just why they can't get anything steady. No. Well, Mike's something like it's in the city. Yeah. They know how to handle it or put the people in the city. It's a one-sided deal or what? Well, I haven't heard Mike play too much, but I heard him a few times.

Yeah, he plays alright, but there's something like it. Some of it is. You know he drives a pony around? He's got a pony and a car and drives him around the channel. Yeah. That gets his kicks. I'm not done. Well, what happens at the New Orleans Jazz Club when you go up there to play? How does that work? I never have played there. I haven't played in years, so I don't know. I used to play a couple of games.

Well, sometimes the boys sort of, like Dutch Andrews and a few others, they sort of pick something in there and they ask you if you want to play. If they happen to hear the trumpet or the clarinet man, hey, they go in the audience stand. They make an announcement for a trumpet man or somebody and they form a group and off they go.
Just like that, just jamming, huh? Yeah, jamming.
I mean, any number that they all agree upon, I guess.
Do you ever get any jobs up there by meeting guys and stuff? Nothing.
No, I was always on my own most of the time.
Well, I guess you're always steady with some of them for years and years. I had a lot of offers and all, but I mean.
I didn't try to push myself, you know, too far. But probably he had a pen, man. I got it on my mind.

I got it on my mind. Yeah. Do you remember there were some kids from Florida, I think, in the radio, a studying radio or something, and they made some tapes up here back in 1950 at American Legion at the Plum Plant. Yeah, I remember Don. I saw him last night.

He's doing okay. He's working at WDSU TV. Is it late? Yeah, he runs a motion picture projector and stuff. You know, he was always like tape machines and motion picture projectors and stuff like that. So he's there. I saw him last night and he might have to tell us what happened to those kids. And who came to the American Legion there? I mean, we had Don and me and a few people. Nick. Who? Nick?
Nick, what was his name? Stuck at the G. Gagliano?
Yeah. Yeah, he liked it. Yeah.
And a lot of musicians came out there.
Jazz fans, some jazz fans. Yeah, Harry Shields, he came out there like.
I'm like, you know, Fugirot, Almarico. But most of the people that just came to that, just from neighborhoods, from uptown, downtown, over the river.
They came from all over. And then the war broke out.

They were, well, planes. Sometimes a dollar, a dollar and a half. And they were on a commission. And then the war broke out. They were, was making between $25 and $30 a man a night. Was that from the kiddie? No, just from the kiddie. It was a 60-40 deal.
Oh, oh, I see. You were on a percentage, huh? Yeah.
And then the union stepped in and said, no, you all have to play for the scale, which was $13 at the time. So, we had to play for the scale. Like we had some, we had some fine crowds there.
Did they always charge to get in? Yeah.
I think it was 50 or 60 cents per man, about 35 cents per woman. Yeah. It was a good deal.
Oh, it was fun. It was a good band. Good women's section, good arms. You read arrangements too, I don't know. You read and you play by ear too?

Yeah, we were starting, we were jamming. They had the waltzes in between. That's what we were doing on the other side. It was the same thing. You see, about every fourth set we hit a waltz. We can like a medley. If we have no requests, well, we just play medleys maybe, anything we feel like. We had to play it in a long time, we play in the form of a medley.
And you play, would you play a slow one and a fast one, a waltz, a slow one and a fast one? How would that work?

We just, we see a slow one and a fast one. Or a slow and a medium one. And say about the fourth set is a waltz and that's a fast one. And then the couple, you know, most sets than that is intermission. And we go back to the oil route and the slow one and the fast one again. And what time do you start? Well, on a Friday from 8.30 to 1.30. On a Saturday from 8.30 to 2.30. And on a Sunday from 8 until 1. We had a pretty nice frowl Sunday but Saturday was a little slack. I mean, you know, cold and the weather just linked in on us and... I mean, they sort of threw some of them. Yeah, well I guess that hurt you. Yeah, and after they get adjusted to it then you'll see them. Does Christmas hurt you? I don't know. Oh. Oh, see just before Christmas it's sort of slow. Like right now it's slowed up some. I have noticed it for last year it's the same way. Yeah. And it's also the same around Easter time and Lent and so forth. It slows down some. And after that, I mean, a lot of folks do take their vacations and all that. Why do you put that limit on your life?
Why do you put that list of tens up there?

Well, just to remind them that we're open for requests and so forth. And then some of the latest numbers. We've got three new ones up there now. I'm not part of the majority of the numbers myself. I don't know anything about buying them. Until you have no more pocket.
Do you get a lead sheet or do you buy a stock around them? No, just the piano sheet. Mm-hmm.
Sort of read the horn now for good transposer. You know, the tone on it. Mm-hmm.
And you read it. Well, you can read from the piano sheets without any trouble or anything? No, there's no trouble there.
No chance as well, isn't it?
Yeah, just the tone on it. That's all.

If it was an E flat, you know, B flat instruments, you put it in that. If it's a G, you put it in A. It's always tone on it. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm sure there's two good. I hate it over there. What if I cover the view things, eh? Yeah, you... About the end of it that way? Yeah, it's the end of that reel. Can you do another one? Oh, I don't know. Well, I mean, I've got a lot of questions if you can answer. Oh, that's good. You got time? Yeah, we're time to do. It's about the end of it that way. Yeah, it's the end of that reel.
Can you do another one? Oh, I don't know. Well, I mean, I've got a lot of questions if you can answer.
Oh, that's good. You got time?
Yeah, we're time to do. It's about 20 minutes. Thank you.
Here we go. We're on reel three of Luke's Giro. And we were talking about legends and the different tunes and things there. What are the people like there mostly? What kind of tunes they

would ask you for? Well, if they ask for some of the new ones and some of the old ones, some Latin American. It all depends on the crowd. Then you might get an Italian ship in there with some seamen and they'll ask for all the Italian numbers. And all we know is a few of them, like Omarie and Osolamé and a few others. So we tried to please them. And then we had a few numbers like trees and Martha and all, which are a fine number. We sort of played those too. That's our numbers and sometimes they ask for them too. And sometimes they ask for some of the real old ones like Mary Lou, Angry, Tin Roof Blues, High Society or March
of the Bobcats. I know she plays a solo song in March of the Bobcats.

Yeah. See, sometimes I poop out on it. I mean, it has to be a certain, you know, tempo for me. But it's not just right. I mean, it has to be right there. The rhythm and all has to be just right, you know. And I can really hit at it. How fast do you like to play?
Well, what's the fastest you ever like to play on? Well, it all depends on the tune.

Oh, see, sometimes like after you're going like the real things, you know. And, I mean, we can look at the old, it's something like a show tune, in other words, I like to. Or, and, let's see, we have a little arrangement there with four numbers that we play. And I think, you see, the, we see the, we see the first number is, let's see, the Lady of Spain. And then we end up with, you know, Carol Ann in the end. And it's real nice. And in between there's a couple of other tunes. I can't remember the names of them. You play that fast? I mean, it's about, it is real fast, but I mean, it's fast enough that, I mean, you'd have
to really, yeah. Well, stomp off how fast you play after you've gone. Give me the beat, this gentleman. That fast? Uh-huh. You get going on a number like that. Oh, yeah. And then we, you know,

sort of play with a lot of numbers. We have about, oh, about a thousand tunes up there. And, some of them may hardly ever get to play. I mean, sometimes if it's slow that night, we'll sort of go through the books then, you know, sort of make a few medallers. And, boy, it's really, I mean, it's really nice. It's, you know, sort of, you know, brace the monotony.
Some nights do you play nearly all requests? Yeah.

Don't get a chance to do it, yeah. No. Sometimes there's a lot of, there's repeats on numbers, like Release Me and, you know, if you're the, you know, terms like Born Free and Born to Lose and you're cheating hard. But that Release Me, boy, that's been, we didn't really ask for that number.
What about the people that come there? Are they married?

Some are married, some divorced, some their husbands died, or their wives died, or they had some hardships somewhere along the line and they couldn't get along. And I usually make my rounds at the table, see what they want, and they usually, they usually help me all their affairs and all, which, I'm a pretty good listener. I don't try to advise them either way, though, because I'll get to trouble. Yeah, you end up in the middle. Yeah, in the middle, that's right. That was it. Okay. I had enough that night on St. Ann's Street when I almost got shot. Another one grabbing the door, that. Where was, where was that?
The Golden Dragon, I think it was. Oh, on, not on St. Ann's. Yeah, the Golden Dragon. That was on St. Ann's Street. I got the tears, man. I guess that's a lot. Man.

But you could write a book, huh? I could really write a book on that. If I knew how to write, I mean, if I knew how to, you know, put the words together, have the ideas, but not exactly how you should go. Each table has a different story. And I think I'm pretty well liked on that. But there's a particular, between that and a few, you know, folks always ask me, I'd like the way I play it. That's, let's see what close the walk would be. I really like that particular tune. That's a real, a popular name. In between, like, Sister Kate and High Society and Sweet Sue, all so many old numbers. How old are the people in my life? Well, believe it or not, there's an old man there. His first name is Gerald. He just had the break there, I think, November the 4th. He made 106 years old. I want to meet him. I got to meet him at his endings. That's right. And then I asked him, how did he, you know, just put, he could do to, he said, just normal living. He said he had an uncle. He said he had an uncle that was 132 years old. I don't know, it's a little, I mean, a little far-fetched. I don't know. But he looks, I mean, fine because he's so, on his birthday, I mean, he wasn't at his birthday, but about a week after he came. So, I called some girl and danced with him. She must have been around. He's about 47 or 48 years old. And, you know, she danced this over the waves with him. She said, I don't want no slow walls, it has to be fast, like over the waves. So, okay, we're playing part of those camp, really. I mean, he really danced. And he enjoyed himself. He's got a good one at that, huh? Yeah, but he wasn't feeling so hot last week, he said. He said, but there's a lot of violence right now. But they got him there from 18 all the way up to 106. So you take your picture.

Well, I've never seen many 18-year-olds. Aren't they most? No, none. They might ask him because they usually ask him the age, you know, that they can't produce. Most of the people don't seem to be 18, 19, so.

No, the majority of them are in the 40s, 50s, 60s, on up. Did you ever go to the old legends that Almanaster and Murray? No, just one time, because at the time I was over at the Legion, I couldn't get down there where I wanted to. I used to hear a lot about it. I mean, after the dance hall was shut over there, a lot of the Legion there, they went down there for their kicks.

Well, they had old people in there, that's right. Only place I ever heard of Big Al Lewis. I knew it. How did he die? That's where I knew it. How long did he die? He died in 49. 49. Yeah, he made those records and played for about two weeks before he died. Yeah, I think. You know? No, I think not. What about the Sweet Potato Inn? You never did tell me much about that.

Well, there was a homebrew joint. Al, Durier, he played there. If you should happen to meet Al, he could sort of breathe on that. It was similar to the Naubeville Street or Abedville Street. And they had the Whip there too, somewhere else in one. That's where Lillard Primmer played for a while. And Lillard Primmer also played at the Frolic, which was on San Yen and Braw there. Lillard Buzzover played there. I played a few spots before the Lillard, but I don't know.
And the Vanity, did you ever go to the Vanity?

Yeah, they had a fine old band there. There was a trombone man. I think his name was Rodney Ogle. He had a band there for a while. A real fine trombone man. I don't know who. No, he was from out of town. Not many luck. And they had the Silver Slipper with Abed Brunners. And Fred Dan Taggart, he played sax there. And I was on Susan Poon. Ed Buzzover was there. And all Rod Paul was there. Sax man, he quit playing. He played like Hopkins. He's selling real estate.
How did you get your saxophone style? Do you think you played like anybody?

No. Just a plain old melody. I don't know if somebody has to tell me that. I haven't analyzed myself. I haven't tried to cop anybody's style. I just... Just hanging around the melody and that's it, you know?
Well, you know, I stop and I think about the different saxophone players that I heard. I heard Edie Miller and Lester Lushon here. Oh yeah, Ed Lushon.

I never heard Lester Nelson. They say he was good. Yeah, he was good. He and Australia used to team up things. Oh yeah. And what was another saxophone? I think they had three, sometimes they had three tenner sometimes. Oh, some big.
Well, the Blue Press Topping used to have arrangements like that for three tenner. Yeah.

Oh, you see I played with Blue a good while back then. I used to substitute them. He had a fine little band. His theme song was the, I think it was Rhapsody and Blue. You know, just... Mm-hmm. And he had a fine little band. He used to get a lot of work. He was more, you know, polished and polished. He had more education. He was more than a kid than a kid. He seemed like a guy so young too. He had a lot of work. He's got one sister left now. Mm-hmm.
Well, his name was Lewis.
Yeah. His name was Lewis.
Is that the one that was married to Joe Rodas, that sister?
No, it was Ervin Fasola was married to Joe Rodas' sister.
Oh, I got it straight now. Yeah. Yeah, well I guess that's the one I met. Yeah.
The little boy said I'd never get married. Mm-hmm. You never did? No, he said I'll never get married.
But he did. Yeah, he did, yeah.
He married Joe Rodas' sister.
Oh, yeah. Wow. No, I got it straight. Because I sat next to her one night and we went to hear Elect Jones. Yeah. Yeah, it was a surprise to meet him. What's that?
She was real nice too. Yeah.
And Fas was a nice fellow to me. I just met him once. Yeah, he was alright.
He was one of the best up-known. I mean, he liked, you know what I mean?
He said, give me a shirt off of this guy. He had a big heart. Yeah. I met him out on the Airline Highway. I can't remember the name of the gentleman. I didn't think of it.

I used to substitute for him when I was in the World Globe, like the Two Tonys on Canal Boulevard there. His theme song was The Boulevard of Broken Dreams. I played every now and then just to play this. You're a nice tune. It is. It's pretty.
Who was in the band at the Two Tonys?
I don't know. I think he's playing with the Tomorrow of Mine on the piano. What's his name again? Charlie Duke was on drums and all that.
I don't know who's at the Tomorrow of Mine.
Heard a piano man.
Well, Jerry Aspinel was out there for a while, but I don't know. He used to play with the Dawn Busters too.
In fact, Foss was with the Dawn of Busters, Al White and all of them.

Did you ever play with Andre and Le Fay? Yeah, he played fine piano. I never really get to hear him except on some homemade record. Yeah, he was real good. He was playing with Johnny Dutroy for a long time. And what about Howard Reed? Did you ever play with him? A trumpet player? No. A trumpet player. See, I may have a good... Yeah, he played with Foss for a while. Yeah, yeah. That's right. Yeah, yeah. He did. He and I did La Fay both played. Julian Lane, he died too. Yeah. He played a lot of T-God type of stuff. Yeah. And Sharky had a good band when he was over at the Hollywood Dance Hall.

I saw him on St. Claude and Lee Fields there at the time. I miss my Schweigman's icon. There was an open air dance hall there. He had Shilang on drums, Frank Pinero on piano, Sherman on bass. He had Nina Pecconi on sax. He quit playing. He was What the World on the Ed Hall. And there was... He did, but you know Winstein on alto and Fazzola was on alto. Nina Pecconi was on tenor. And then they got... He was the Amaya Linebrier. He was on sax too. Fine sax man. He played Prim a while too. Yeah, I heard him on the record. And the Ed... I think Freddie Wright Cannon was singing. He was playing guitar. And I think they got Sharky and Leon or Prim on trumpets. They had a fine band. Yeah. Yeah. Well I think there are pictures in this book, this New Orleans Jazz, a family album by Al Rose and Ed Van Souci. And I'll try to find that picture but... How about that picture up there? Is it up there? No. I don't think we got a picture up there. I got it on me.
Other one. Other. Other. Other picture with Bob Aguilar. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Bob Aguilaro.
They got a picture of Aguilaro in here. Yeah, that's right.
With Schilling, wasn't it with Schilling?
Yeah, with Schilling. Yeah, Schilling was playing guitar, which I'd forgotten that he played guitar.
Yeah, he played guitar and trombone, didn't he?
Yeah, and he hired him to talk about trombone. And then his son also played.
Didn't he have a son at the Big Sags?
How was Vazola's tone on the sax? The sax, fine.
He had a good, he had a cool tone. But that clad was the best tone. He used a stiff read to him on a three and a half.

Well, you see, I never heard him play sax, really, except maybe in the section. Here's this band at the Little Club. Prima Chalkman, the orchestra, 1930. With Charlie Hawkman on the trombone. Oh yeah, Charlie Hawkman was a good band. I told him on that. Chalky Leon, Prima, Foss, Winstyn, Unifacon. Yeah, what's his setup? Same setup, Schilling. Yeah, same setup, Louis Macenton too, but I had Sussaphone. Yeah, he was a single, but he also played string bass too. Yeah, and Freddie Locano's got a banjo in the picture. Yeah. And Frank Benares at the piano. Yeah, that's right. Same band, just a band. Same band. I think it was a same band. Exactly. But somebody came in on sax too. Maya Weinberg. Yeah, what did he play, tenor or alto? Alto. Alto.
Alto and Clarinet. He played a fine clarinet.
And what happened to him? I don't know. He was almost...
I attacked him. He was playing with, uh... I wasn't even a good while back before he became famous. Louis Prima, a lot of times, used to make a lot of records.

Yeah, they even played the verse to the one in a row. I think it's if I could be with you. I don't know what it surprised me if they came up with a verse or something like that. Yeah. Which they don't do much anymore. No, they don't. People don't play verse. Did they play verse as much when you started?
Yeah. A good while back, yeah. I guess you read some. Yeah.
You'd read them.
Yeah, we did a lot of reading there. Yeah. The introduction and then the chorus of the voice and then the last chorus. Sometimes it was real good, we used to play all the way through, you know.
Let's stop it for a minute so we can watch the television for just... I want you to catch one number of our hokey.

The Heroes, you know? Yeah. You like the Heroes and stuff? I used to like... I mean, after they came back, you know, the way they played, you know. Mm-hmm. It was really set. Yeah. And then those bands used to come out the front of my house and just buck each other for hours. Mm-hmm. For about a couple hours, yeah. Yeah.
What about when you were going out on the selling ice cream, where did you sell ice cream? I was in the old Red Light District there.

Mm-hmm. And I heard a lot of good bands out there too. Joe Robichio, to hear... I saw the trumpet man, that's the downtown, yeah, on the Coliseum. Oh yeah, he hit Renee. Mm-hmm. He played a fine trumpet. He drank a lot of wine. He killed him.
About what year would it be you would be going around the District? Oh, well, 1929, 30, all the way up to 37, I believe. Mm-hmm.
And after that, they shut it down or something. And they made a housing project out of it. Yeah. So about 37 was closed down. See, about that time. I don't know. Mm-hmm.
And when did they build that housing project in there? I can't remember whether that was before the war or during the war. Mm-hmm.
It was before the war. Before the war. I'm not quite sure it was. Mm-hmm.
I wasn't down there, but I heard people go to the war. I mean, it was real.
I think they should have another one like that down in the office. It was a big help, you know.
It helped business and all, you know. brought a lot of people in the town, I guess, the sailors. And the sailors and all the businessmen coming from. That's right.

It was a real good deal. I mean, it was from Iberville to Basie Street. It was all the way up to North Robeson and then to St. Louis Street. They had Eclipse Alley in there. And I made a lot of money back there. So I was well-liked and I was known back there. And then they had another little other district up further. I mean, Saab Robeson all the way up to, I guess, Padres Street. And then I made that route also. And I was pretty well-known on town, too.
How far up towards the river did that district go? Well, I mean... It's up there.
They had some houses on the other. The Burgundy and the Burgundy Street. And so...
You know, I mean on the other side of the canal.

Oh, as far as, let's see, that block on the other side of the canal, it was Cleveland. They had a few there and some on South Robeson. And then I got on Saabert and Toba Street. The colored folks up there. They used to call them... They had another street that used to call, you know, Cleveland. And then they had another old neighborhood, Gasket Street. And then all the way up to Pardner Street. And they had the banana sheds back there. They had those banana... They had these schooners and all. They had these watermelon schooners and they had these... They had all sorts of banana... Knocked out the boats. They had these...
Freight cars with bananas, you know, in there. Is that around the new basin you're talking about?
Around the new basin, yeah. And they had bass women there, Hustlin women and stuff. Yeah, they had them all on there. The majority of them were colored.
Would it go up to Rampart Street?
Yeah, South Rampart Street.

All along South Rampart. All the way over Pardner Street. And then St. Louis Street. And then down South Rampart Street. And then all the way down there. And St. Louis Street. Where they go up to Drys?

That close end of the road? Yeah, they had a few of them up there too. Barone? Yeah, Barone Street. That was after them. Yeah. Oh yeah, well that was... And then they scattered all around town then. We had them in the neighborhoods and all, no? Yeah. But they had some as far as...
Burden Street, Horton, Ties Street, St. Louis, I mean back over Rampart Street. All along North Rampart Street too. What about the women?
Did they like ice cream? Oh yeah, they bought a lot of ice cream.

You know some of them with... They had to put some on a book and I just... I gave it to them. I didn't charge them. And then they finally... Finally they caught a trick or two and they sort of paid me off.
Well I guess they made pretty good money though. Oh yeah, they did. They were charged with them.

They had some nice looking girls back there. It was a shame. But some of them had a bad marriage or something. Or a bad family. Or a family divorce. You know like... The same situation right now I guess.
Yeah. How much would they get for a trick? Short time. Well...

From a dollar on up to three, five the most. They had Lula Whites. They had... They had the Stag Hotel there which was on Basin Street. And there was a view on Franklin Street there. Franklin and Colette Tower. I knew them all. They had Willie Pierre's and she was on Franklin Street. And the front was on Basin Street. And sometimes a lot of musicians would go up there. They had a piano and the piano would play with... Sort of play the balloons or something. Or something soft. They had a piano and they... It was something different. You know? Some of the boys would start going after a job. It was real good.
The place would run all the way through the block from Franklin to Basin. Yeah.
I mean some beautiful homes in there. I mean they were... They had these thick rugs about so thick you know. An inch thick or something? No.
You know, it was a plush street.

Yeah. Like the hotels. And old time chandeliers and furniture and all that. You could smell the incense in there. You know the deal. It was weird. I can still remember. In fact I went up there a lot of times myself. Well you were young though. I mean you were too young. They didn't... How old were you when you started selling ice cream? About 16 or 17. Well you were old enough then. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.

Beautiful little blonde. And she was about 16 years old. She used to like me a lot. An old man found out about it. And he put a stout to it. Yeah. I couldn't stand for that. No. But boy she could dress. And I used to dress at the time myself. I was one of the best dressed in the city. I mean for amateur musicians at the time. And you know. And that. See Alna Riega was also a real good dresser. They used to have around eight tailor made suits, about 75 Irish shirts with other accessories, and about three or four silk shirts. And then over 100 times, every week, I mean I sort of go to Rubenstein and sit with someone on the other side, on that street then. And every week I sort of get me with necktie and a shirt to match and socks, and that was it. And the old man was sitting, what, another shirt to tie? What you want to do? You made enough money selling ice cream. Oh, you used to make around three or four hundred dollars a week at the time. I thought it was going to last forever.
Well that's a lot of money. Everything went bad then, I mean.
The old man went bankrupt and so forth. In the meantime, I got married and had a gang of children and that was it.
When did you get married with me?
I was about 18 years old.
That would mean about the time of the Depression then?

Yeah. I was staying in one room, five dollars a month. Five dollars a month? There was a room about this size. There was no electricity. The water was in the back. Had a number three tough to take a bath in. You had to wash everything by hand. You know, it was a washboard deal. And the voice ball was born in the house there. On Barracks and Liberty. I'll never forget that. At the time I was playing on Decatur Street at the Roman Cafe.
What year would that be when you went to Roman? 19...
36, 35, something like that.
You had to wait a while then in those years before you hadn't been a kid. Yeah, no, gee. Let's see. We had nine kids all the time. That's a lot. This set of twins in there.

Really, it's been a struggle but I enjoyed every bit of it. I don't know. You know, raising kids. Now we have about 24 grandchildren. So, I think, you see they're expecting another one around January. Which would be about 25. So, like I said, it's all in the game.
Could you buy many records then? When you were growing up? Were you making that kind of money? Did you buy many?

Yeah, I mean at the time I used to get these old care records. You know, Longstrong and Big Spyback and a few other ones. And, you see I loaned a lot from those records. I mean, you helped a lot. And I loaned them to Louis Primm. I never did get them back, the Longstrong records. That was the end of them. He was always conniving for something. He got it in his own way. He was alright though. I remember when he used to play the cornet. And he used to play the violin. He played a good violin. When he was going to Aloysius school there.

I never did hear him play violin. No. I don't guess he made a good record. No, he never even made a good record. Was he a hot violin player? Yeah. A straight man. Hot, he got all the way. Did they have many hot violin players there?
They had a few of them. They had this... Was it Mickey Marker? No, Mickey was a piano player. Yeah, a piano player. Which one was it? Oscar.
Oscar. I knew him.

I met him before he died. I heard him play one time. Jeremy Christian. Heard me? I don't know him. No, they didn't hear. They had these other Christians. They all played violin and trombone or something like that. Well, Emil I know.
They tell me Frank is still living. Yeah, Frank. Yeah, there's nothing.
I mean the majority of them were on the WP at the time.
Was Herbie came to them?
Yeah. I can't remember. He was with the dance band. He was with Emmanuel Sanders Band. Charlie Goodell.
Could he get off?

Well, some, but I mean he did a lot of reading most of them. He was really good. He got a good tone out of his violin. Oh, so many of them. I mean they had the symphony, they had the military bands, they had the dance band, and they had the recreation band with Cliff Curry. They had Pete Bacopa, he had a little outfit.
That's all that he had? Yeah.

And I mean all of the best musicians in the city were there. I mean they had the first class, the second class. I was second class. He didn't like the DLs, he like the professor, the Bacopa was in there, and a few other professors. And the old man Fontana had the symphony, and Sabatis took over, he was a violin player. And then, you see every Wednesday night we'd sort of play out City, Park, Nave, and we'd consolidated all the bands. And we'd have, we'd play his overtures like Wigantale, New Travica and so forth. And at the end of the night we'd, the last half hour we'd have a jam session. I'm going to play the violin myself and Arthur Sealy and the Raymond. I think I'm going to pick myself there.
Yeah, well the tape's about to run out. I think we can go on another one if you've got the time. No. Yeah, well I could block the questions.
I'm alright.
Yeah, but uh... Yeah.
24 Houses
Wait a minute, we're going now. This is Rio 4, of Luke Skiro, December 5, 1967. You were talking about the Orleanians and you used to play around?
Yeah, around the houses, you know. House parties and so forth.
And who was in that band? Oh. It doesn't matter if you can't think of it.
It's been so long ago.
Listen, what was the Blue Horseshoe like? I got this record, Stopping at the Blue Horseshoe by Fazzola.
Oh, the Blue Horseshoe was a place, you know something like these Moteldi, you know you take a girl out there and if you, you know it's a deal.
Yeah, I get that.
Something like that. Well, it's the Blue Horseshoe. I lost you, Jesus.
